analysis.one_liner: Overhauls federal workplace safety law: mandatory safety programs, worker safety committees, higher fines, and coverage for state and local government workers.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the House committee on October 3, 1994 with 138 cosponsors, but never received a floor vote before Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the 1970 law that governs workplace safety. It would require employers with 11 or more workers to run written safety programs and set up joint worker-management safety committees, extend federal safety coverage for the first time to state and local government employees and federal nuclear facilities, let workers refuse dangerous work without being fired, and raise both civil and criminal penalties for safety violations, including personal criminal liability for company officers. It would also require faster limits on toxic exposures and the first federal standard on repetitive-strain (ergonomic) injuries.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers gain the most: about 7 million state and local government employees would get federal safety protection they currently lack, construction workers would get dedicated inspections and training programs, and workers everywhere would gain the right to safety committees, to refuse imminent dangers without retaliation, and to contest settlements their employers cut with regulators. Families of workers killed or hurt on the job would get formal rights in enforcement proceedings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, especially public employees and construction crews

how_it_helps.text: Extends OSHA coverage to state and local government employees, who are currently excluded from the federal safety law, and applies it to Department of Energy nuclear facilities [S2][S4].

Requires every employer with 11 or more workers to establish a written safety and health program and a joint safety committee with elected employee representatives, with quarterly worksite inspections by the committee [S2][S4].
Lets employees refuse work identified as an imminent danger without being fired, and extends anti-retaliation protection to anyone reporting an injury, illness, or unsafe condition [S2].

Raises penalties sharply: minimum $1,000 fines for serious violations, $10,000-$50,000 per day for ignoring an imminent-danger notice, prison terms up to 20 years for willful violations causing death, and new criminal penalties for willful violations causing serious bodily injury — with officers and supervisors personally liable and barred from paying fines out of company assets [S4].

Directs OSHA to issue the 1989 air-contaminant exposure limits within 60 days and a first-ever ergonomic injury standard within two years, and to update toxic exposure limits at least every three years [S2][S4].

Establishes construction-specific safety offices, an inspection academy, and a toll-free complaint line, and gives workers and their families rights to contest inadequate citations and settlements [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers bear the cost: writing safety programs, training workers on paid time, running committees, monitoring toxic exposures and medical surveillance, paying higher fines, and facing personal criminal liability for managers. Small employers get targeted assistance but also new mandates, and companies receiving OSHA consultation services would pay fees into a new fund.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall hardest on small firms: the bill mandates written programs, committees, training, exposure monitoring, and recordkeeping for every employer with 11 or more workers, and imposes fees for OSHA assistance services [S2][S4].

Managers and supervisors face personal criminal prosecution and personal fines (which cannot be paid by the company) for safety failures, up to 10-20 years in prison for willful violations — a liability expansion that even safety-minded businesses opposed [S4].

Employers contesting serious citations could no longer delay fixing the hazard while fighting the citation, except through a formal stay showing likelihood of success — removing a flexibility businesses valued [S4].

Employers lose citations only under a new 'employee accountability' defense if they can prove training, work rules, and enforcement — a partial concession, but one that shifts burden of proof onto the employer [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are real but concentrated: employers, particularly small ones and those in construction and manufacturing, would absorb new mandates, fees, and liability. The benefits are spread across every covered workplace — fewer deaths, injuries, and toxic exposures, and the first safety floor for public employees. A reasonable objection is that the bill layered many new mandates at once rather than prioritizing the highest-hazard workplaces; the bill itself partially answers this by targeting inspections and assistance at the most dangerous sites and offering small-business assistance, but the aggregate compliance burden was the core of the opposition.

outcome.mechanism: The House Education and Labor Committee approved and reported the bill on October 3, 1994, but House leaders never brought it up for a vote before Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

narrative.text: Introduced March 10, 1993 by Rep. William Ford of Michigan and referred to the Education and Labor and House Administration Committees [S6].

The bill drew 138 cosponsors — 136 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 1 Republican — and received multiple committee and subcommittee hearings through 1994, including executive comments from the Labor Department [S5][S6].
The subcommittee was discharged and the full committee marked the bill up in March 1994, ordering it reported as amended [S6].
The committee reported the bill to the House on October 3, 1994 (H. Rept. 103-825, Part I), five weeks before the midterm election [S3][S6].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a House floor vote and died when the 103rd Congress ended [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers — particularly small businesses, contractors, and manufacturers — came out ahead, avoiding new safety committees, higher fines, personal criminal liability for executives, and the extension of federal safety rules to government workplaces. The workers the bill would have protected gained nothing.

industries.note: The bill imposes written safety programs, mandatory committees, exposure monitoring, and higher fines on any employer with 11 or more workers. Its cost is the compliance burden; its purpose is fewer workplace deaths and injuries.

A dedicated construction safety office, inspector academy, mandatory project safety coordinators, targeted inspections, and reporting requirements for fatalities and structural failures fall directly on contractors. Construction has among the highest workplace fatality rates, which is why the bill singles it out.

Small employers get targeted technical assistance, model programs, and consultation services designed for them, but they also face the same program, committee, and recordkeeping mandates and would pay fees for OSHA assistance under the new OSHA Assistance Fund.

Criminal penalties would extend beyond the corporate employer to officers, managers, and supervisors personally, with fines that cannot be paid out of company assets and prison terms up to 20 years for willful violations causing death.
